qdi1jemn.name: Lipidology: decision support

rows.t: What has happened, what is inherited, what has been tried?
Events set the risk tier; family history flags FH and Lp(a); therapy history separates non-adherence from intolerance
Is something else driving the lipids?
Common and often reversible; the pattern (LDL vs TG) points at the cause
TSH, UACR, A1c, LFTs, drug review
Are there physical signs of a lipid disorder or of atherosclerosis?
Specific signs reclassify (FH criteria, remnant disease, chylomicronemia); bruits move the patient into secondary prevention
What do we measure, and when?
Standard panel plus apoB and a once-only Lp(a); CAC settles the undecided primary-prevention case
The phenotype determines drug choice, family implications and pancreatitis risk
Who else in the family is affected?
FH and Lp(a) are co-dominant: half of first-degree relatives; finding them early changes lifetime risk
Tier sets intensity and the threshold for adding non-statins
Which drug, what dose, what interacts?
Potency and interactions explain most failures and most harms
Is it really intolerance, and are they taking it?
Nocebo and non-adherence outnumber true myopathy many-fold; a structured rechallenge settles it
Is this a risk problem or a pancreatitis problem?
Moderate HTG is an apoB/remnant risk marker; severe HTG is a pancreatitis emergency with its own diet and drugs
Liver disease, diabetes, pregnancy, age, kidney disease and HIV change drug choice or thresholds, not the logic
What do we measure, and when?
Timing and the right marker (apoB/non-HDL in TG-dominant patients) separate real failure from non-adherence
What is this logic resting on?
Each row elsewhere should trace to a source here

qdi1jemn.sub: Disease-state node. Guideline-level (ACC/AHA 2018 + 2022 ECDP; ESC/EAS 2019; NLA statements; AHA 2021 HTG), not patient-specific. Layer 0 = the questions a lipid evaluation must answer, in the order they change management. Review against primary sources (see Sources) before clinical use.

cxdwk0xn.name: History

rows.t: MI, PCI/CABG, stroke/TIA, PAD, revascularization, angina; dates
Clinical ASCVD puts the patient in secondary prevention regardless of LDL level
High-intensity statin; LDL threshold for add-on 70 (55 if very high risk)
Premature ASCVD, high cholesterol, pancreatitis in relatives
Diet pattern (saturated fat, refined carbohydrate, alcohol), activity, weight trajectory, smoking
Diet moves LDL ~10%, TG far more; alcohol and carbohydrate are TG drivers
Lifestyle prescription; TG-specific diet if TG high
Which drugs, doses, responses, symptoms, CK
Distinguishes non-adherence, nocebo and true intolerance
Cold intolerance/weight gain (thyroid), oedema (nephrotic), pruritus/jaundice (cholestasis), polyuria (diabetes), alcohol intake
Treating the cause may fix the lipids
Full list incl. OTC and hormones
Many drugs raise LDL or TG or interact with statins
Women: menopause, pregnancy plans, oral estrogen
Oral estrogen raises TG; pregnancy changes drug choice

cxdwk0xn.sub: The lipid history answers three things: what has already happened (events), what is inherited (family), and what has been tried (therapy and tolerance). Everything else is confirmation.

qtcsbn3y.name: Family history

rows.t: Risk enhancer; raises suspicion of FH or Lp(a)
Measure Lp(a); consider CAC in intermediate risk
Relative with LDL ≥190 or known FH
50% of first-degree relatives of an FH proband are affected
Relative with pancreatitis or very high TG
TG workup; genetic testing if TG >1000 from childhood
Sudden cardiac death, aortic stenosis at young age

qtcsbn3y.sub: Premature ASCVD or very high LDL in a first-degree relative is a risk enhancer and the entry point to cascade screening.

y1ollbc1.name: Prior therapy and tolerance

rows.t: Each statin tried: dose, duration, response (LDL before/after)
Response tells you adherence and potency
High-intensity should lower LDL ≥50%; much less suggests non-adherence or absorption
Symptoms: what, where, onset after start, resolution after stop, recurrence on rechallenge
Symmetric proximal myalgia within weeks that resolves in 2–4 weeks off and recurs on rechallenge is more credible than vague fatigue
CK >10× ULN with symptoms = stop; most "intolerance" has normal CK
Why stopped: cost, side effect, belief, advice
Cost and nocebo are the commonest reasons

y1ollbc1.sub: "Failed statins" is a history to take, not a label to accept. Which drug, what dose, what happened, what was measured.

vqtkpe1d.name: Secondary causes of dyslipidemia

rows.t: Replete before judging LDL; statin myopathy risk higher when hypothyroid
Treat the renal disease; statin still often needed
Statin ± ezetimibe (SHARP); do not start statin on dialysis
LpX not atherogenic in the usual way; xanthomas common
ApoB or non-HDL tracks risk better than LDL

vqtkpe1d.sub: Screen in everyone before starting therapy; the pattern (LDL-dominant vs TG-dominant) points at the cause.

tla9kkm5.name: Drugs that worsen lipids

rows.t: HDL is a marker, not a target
Net effect generally favourable; apoB unchanged

tla9kkm5.sub: Stop or switch when possible; otherwise treat around them.

zr3qlmnx.name: Examination

rows.t: Achilles (thickened, nodular), extensor tendons of hands; look and palpate
Pathognomonic for FH (Dutch criteria 6 points); also sitosterolemia, CTX
Non-specific; ~half have dyslipidemia; independent risk marker
Lipid panel; FH criterion if young
Crops of yellow papules with red base on buttocks, extensors, back
Carotid / femoral bruits, diminished pulses, ABI
Auscultate; ABI if symptoms or risk
Subclinical or clinical atherosclerosis = reclassify to higher risk
Metabolic syndrome components; risk calculator inputs

zr3qlmnx.sub: Signs are uncommon but specific: a tendon xanthoma or arcus before 45 is an FH criterion; eruptive xanthomas mean chylomicrons; palmar crease xanthomas mean remnant disease.

30pb8le5.name: Testing

rows.t: Standard panel (TC, TG, HDL, calculated LDL)
Baseline; 4–12 weeks after any change; then 3–12 monthly
Non-fasting acceptable unless TG >400 or TG-focused evaluation
Friedewald unreliable when TG >400 (use Martin/Hopkins or direct LDL)
Captures all apoB particles; secondary target 30 mg/dL above LDL goal
Baseline in most; always with TG-dominant pattern
CK only if symptoms or high myopathy risk
Creamy supernatant = chylomicrons; turbid infranatant = VLDL
≥2 mg/L supports treatment in borderline risk
Plaque reclassifies upward; IMT alone not recommended
Alternative to CAC in some settings

30pb8le5.sub: A standard panel, plus apoB and a once-in-a-lifetime Lp(a). Imaging answers the "should I treat?" question when the calculator cannot.

v4ks9q93.name: Apolipoprotein B

rows.t: Risk refinement when TG 150–499, diabetes, obesity
Discordance: LDL at goal but apoB high = residual risk
<80 high risk; <65 very high risk (ESC); NLA similar
Prefer apoB or non-HDL for follow-up in TG-dominant patients
Order once baseline, then as the follow-up target

v4ks9q93.sub: One particle, one apoB. Better than LDL-C when particles are small and numerous (diabetes, metabolic syndrome, high TG) and for discordance.

24xbjjpd.name: Lipoprotein(a)

rows.t: Everyone at least once (NLA 2024, ESC 2019); especially premature ASCVD, FH, family history, aortic stenosis, recurrent events on therapy
≥50 mg/dL or ≥125 nmol/L = risk enhancer; risk rises continuously
Lowers the threshold to start/intensify LDL lowering; cascade testing of relatives
Treat LDL more aggressively; PCSK9i lowers Lp(a) ~25%
Antisense/siRNA agents (pelacarsen, olpasiran, lepodisiran) in phase 3 outcome trials; results reporting 2025–2026 — verify current status
Trial enrolment; lipoprotein apheresis in selected cases
Some LDL-C assays include Lp(a) cholesterol; repeat measurement unnecessary unless assay changes
Do not chase it with niacin

24xbjjpd.sub: Genetically determined, stable for life, measured once. High in ~20% of people and missed by every routine panel.

qo3lvfnn.name: Risk calculators

rows.t: Age 40–79, sex, race, TC, HDL, SBP, treated BP, diabetes, smoking
Adds eGFR, BMI, UACR, A1c, social deprivation index; drops race; age 30–79
Same categories; values ~half of PCE for many
Guideline thresholds were calibrated to PCE; interpret accordingly
Family history, LDL ≥160, metabolic syndrome, CKD, inflammatory disease, premature menopause, pre-eclampsia, South Asian ancestry, TG ≥175, apoB ≥130, Lp(a) ≥50, hs-CRP ≥2, ABI <0.9
High lifetime risk argues for earlier treatment even when 10-year risk is low

qo3lvfnn.sub: Pooled Cohort Equations (2013) and PREVENT (2023) give different numbers; PREVENT runs lower. Use one consistently and treat the number as a conversation, not a verdict.

6bax5yfp.name: Coronary artery calcium scoring

rows.t: Reasonable to defer statin and repeat in 5–10 years — unless diabetes, smoking, family history of premature ASCVD, or LDL ≥190
Present; risk above calculator estimate if <75th percentile
Statin indicated; treat as higher risk
Do not repeat on statin (statins raise CAC density)

6bax5yfp.sub: The tie-breaker for intermediate (7.5–20%) and selected borderline risk when the decision is uncertain.

5fyk3hcs.name: Genetic testing

rows.t: LDL ≥190 (adult) or ≥160 (child) with family history or physical signs; DLCN ≥6
Pathogenic variant in ~60–80% of definite FH; polygenic score explains most of the rest
TG >1000 from childhood, recurrent pancreatitis, no response to fibrates
FCS vs multifactorial chylomicronemia; FCS is eligible for volanesorsen/olezarsen-type therapy where available
Mixed TC/TG elevation with palmar xanthomas
Cheaper and definitive once the family variant is known

5fyk3hcs.sub: Confirms FH, enables cascade testing of relatives, and identifies FCS; a negative test does not exclude polygenic hypercholesterolemia.

f2mrkmhy.name: Lipid phenotypes

rows.t: LDL ≥190 untreated, autosomal dominant family history, tendon xanthomas
High-intensity statin from diagnosis; add ezetimibe/PCSK9i early; cascade screening; statins from age 8–10 in children
LDL >400–500 untreated, xanthomas in childhood, aortic stenosis
Specialist: PCSK9i (if residual LDLR function), lomitapide, evinacumab, apheresis
No variant on testing; high polygenic score
Treat by risk; cascade less yielding
↑apoB with variable LDL/TG, family members with different patterns
ApoB-guided; statin ± fibrate or icosapent ethyl
TC and TG both ~300–600, roughly equal; low apoB relative to TC
ApoE2/E2 plus a second hit (obesity, diabetes, hypothyroidism); palmar/tuberous xanthomas
Highly responsive to fibrate/statin and treating the second hit
TG >1000 from childhood, recurrent pancreatitis, no response to fibrates
Biallelic LPL-pathway variants; very low apoB
Very-low-fat diet (<10–15% energy); apoC-III-targeted therapy where available
TG >1000 in adults with secondary drivers (diabetes, alcohol, drugs, obesity) on a polygenic background
Responds to removing drivers and fibrates
Risk enhancer; intensify LDL lowering; cascade
Often with ↑TG and insulin resistance; rare genetic causes (ABCA1, LCAT, apoA-I)
Not a drug target; address TG and lifestyle
Family pattern; fat-soluble vitamin status if homozygous
Xanthomas with normal/mildly high LDL; macrothrombocytopenia
Ezetimibe is the treatment; avoid plant sterol supplements

f2mrkmhy.sub: Name the disorder before treating the number: the phenotype decides the drug, the family implications and the pancreatitis risk.

4m018jbz.name: Heterozygous FH

rows.t: First-degree relative with premature ASCVD or LDL >95th pct
First-degree relative with tendon xanthoma/arcus, or child <18 with LDL >95th pct
Simon Broome criteria are an alternative; US MEDPED uses age-specific LDL cut-offs

4m018jbz.sub: 1 in ~250–300. Lifelong LDL exposure; untreated men have ~50% CHD risk by 50, women ~30% by 60. Treat early, screen relatives.

qep13hhp.name: Family cascade screening

rows.t: LDL ≥190 (adult) / ≥160 (child), DLCN ≥6, pathogenic variant, premature ASCVD with high LDL
Confirm diagnosis; document the variant if found
Lipid panel (fasting not required); genetic test for the family variant if known
Second-degree relatives of affected first-degree relatives
Continue outward from each new case
From age 2 if FH in the family; universal screening at 9–11 and 17–21 (AAP/NLA)
Lipid panel; LDL ≥160 with family history suggests FH
Statins considered from age 8–10 for HeFH
First-degree relatives of someone with Lp(a) ≥50 mg/dL or premature ASCVD
Siblings and children of FCS proband
Letter the proband can give relatives; patient-led contact; registry where available

qep13hhp.sub: The highest-yield preventive act in lipidology: each FH proband has, on average, several affected relatives who do not know.

kgdddtlp.name: Risk tier and LDL targets

rows.t: LDL ≥100 on maximal statin → ezetimibe → PCSK9i
Moderate; high if multiple risk factors or 10-yr risk ≥20%
Do not initiate on dialysis; continue if already on
Elevated Lp(a) or very high apoB
Treat LDL to a lower tier

kgdddtlp.sub: ACC/AHA uses thresholds for adding therapy; ESC uses explicit goals. Both converge: the higher the risk, the lower the LDL and the earlier the add-on.

muiun64m.name: Clinical ASCVD tiers

rows.t: ≥2 major events (recent ACS <12 mo, MI, ischemic stroke, symptomatic PAD) OR 1 major event + ≥2 high-risk conditions (age ≥65, HeFH, prior CABG/PCI, diabetes, hypertension, CKD, smoking, LDL ≥100 on maximal statin, HF)
High-intensity statin → ezetimibe if LDL ≥70 (2022 ECDP: ≥55) → PCSK9 mAb → bempedoic acid/inclisiran
High-intensity statin; add ezetimibe if LDL ≥70; PCSK9i reasonable if still ≥70 (2022 ECDP)
Continue or start moderate/high intensity after discussion
ASCVD, diabetes with organ damage, eGFR <30, FH with ASCVD, SCORE2 high
LDL <55 and ≥50% reduction; <40 if recurrent event within 2 years

muiun64m.sub: Very high risk = history of multiple major events, or one major event plus multiple high-risk conditions (ACC/AHA 2018).

rwjx6ywh.name: Primary prevention decision

rows.t: Lifestyle; statin if risk enhancers favour
Moderate-intensity statin to lower LDL ≥30%; high intensity if enhancers
Lifestyle; statin if LDL ≥190 or FH; consider if family history + LDL ≥160

rwjx6ywh.sub: The calculator starts the conversation; risk enhancers and CAC finish it.

yapx71zz.name: Clinical pharmacology

rows.t: CYP3A4 and OATP1B1 are the mechanisms
IMPROVE-IT: modest MACE benefit added to simvastatin; no monitoring needed; generic
First add-on after maximal tolerated statin
CLEAR Outcomes: 13% MACE ↓ in statin-intolerant; prodrug activated in liver (no muscle effect); ↑ uric acid/gout, tendon rupture (rare)
After statin + ezetimibe; HeFH; very high risk
REDUCE-IT: 25% MACE ↓ with TG 135–499 on statin (mineral-oil placebo debate); ↑ AF, bleeding
TG 150–499 with ASCVD or diabetes + risk factors
ACCORD-Lipid: benefit only in TG ≥204/HDL ≤34 subgroup; PROMINENT (pemafibrate): no CV benefit; safe with statins (unlike gemfibrozil); ↑ creatinine (reversible)

Outcome trial PREVAIL ongoing — verify status
Phase 3 outcome trials (HORIZON, OCEAN(a)-Outcomes) — verify results

yapx71zz.sub: Potency, interactions and sequencing. Most harm from statins comes from drug interactions with simvastatin and lovastatin, not from statins per se.

abz8g91v.name: Statin intensity (ACC/AHA)

rows.t: Atorvastatin 10–20; rosuvastatin 5–10; simvastatin 20–40; pravastatin 40–80; lovastatin 40–80; fluvastatin XL 80 (or 40 bid); pitavastatin 1–4
Hydrophilic (rosuva, prava) and pitavastatin have fewer CYP3A4 interactions; evening dosing only matters for short half-life statins (simva, lova, flu, prava)

abz8g91v.sub: Daily dose by expected LDL reduction. Doubling a statin dose adds only ~6%.

xrt77vg4.name: Statin drug interactions

rows.t: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors: clarithromycin, erythromycin, itraconazole, ketoconazole, posaconazole, voriconazole, HIV protease inhibitors, cobicistat, nefazodone
Use lowest dose; hold during short antibiotic courses
Limited interaction (cap 10 mg with some PI combinations)
Fenofibrate instead of gemfibrozil with any statin
Prefer rosuva/prava at lower dose, or avoid simva 40–80

xrt77vg4.sub: Simvastatin and lovastatin are CYP3A4 substrates with dose caps; atorvastatin less so; rosuvastatin, pravastatin, pitavastatin and fluvastatin largely avoid CYP3A4. Cyclosporine and gemfibrozil interact with nearly all statins via OATP1B1 and glucuronidation.

1wzwbx09.name: PCSK9-directed therapy

rows.t: 140 mg q2w or 420 mg monthly SC
FOURIER: 15% MACE ↓ over 2.2 y; benefit grows with time (FOURIER-OLE)
ODYSSEY OUTCOMES: 15% MACE ↓, mortality signal; post-ACS
284 mg SC at 0, 3 months, then every 6 months
ORION trials; outcome trial (ORION-4, VICTORION-2P) pending — verify; adherence advantage
Prior authorization: document maximal tolerated statin + ezetimibe and LDL above threshold

1wzwbx09.sub: Monoclonal antibodies and siRNA. Large, safe LDL reductions; the question is access and cost.

cdq8mffv.name: Statin intolerance, nocebo and adherence

rows.t: Inability to tolerate ≥2 statins, one at the lowest approved dose, with symptoms that resolve on stopping and recur on rechallenge; complete vs partial
Requires a structured rechallenge, not a report

Check TSH, vitamin D, renal function

Rare autoimmune entity; do not rechallenge
Wait for resolution (2–4 weeks) → different statin (rosuvastatin or pravastatin, low dose) → alternate-day or twice-weekly rosuvastatin 5–10 mg → add ezetimibe
Lower dose less-interacting statin tolerated by most
Non-statin if still intolerant: ezetimibe → bempedoic acid → PCSK9i
CYP3A4 drugs, hypothyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, age, low BMI, CKD, Asian ancestry (rosuvastatin), heavy exercise, alcohol
Absolute risk reduction, NNT, lifetime LDL exposure

cdq8mffv.sub: In SAMSON, 90% of the symptom burden on statin was also present on placebo. Most "intolerance" is nocebo or non-adherence; true myopathy is rare and recognizable.

nrljx4yl.name: Nocebo effect and n-of-1 trials

Needs a cooperative pharmacy; otherwise open rechallenge with diary
"Statins can cause muscle symptoms in a small minority; most symptoms people notice are not caused by the drug" (not "it is all in your head")

nrljx4yl.sub: Expectation produces symptoms. Blinded rechallenge turns a belief into a measurement.

Generic statin + ezetimibe; single-pill combination; inclisiran for adherence; address beliefs

Once-daily any time of day for atorva/rosuva
Panel 4–12 weeks after start; then 3–12 monthly

d3uwqr0b.name: Hypertriglyceridemia

rows.t: Marker of remnant/apoB burden, insulin resistance
Lifestyle (carbohydrate, alcohol, weight), secondary causes, statin for ASCVD risk
Icosapent ethyl if ASCVD/diabetes + risk factors (REDUCE-IT)
Rising pancreatitis risk; chylomicrons begin to appear
Very low fat diet short-term, stop alcohol, control diabetes, drug review
Fibrate (fenofibrate) or omega-3 4 g; then statin for ASCVD risk
Fat <10–15% of energy, no alcohol, treat triggers
Uncontrolled diabetes, alcohol, oral estrogen, glucocorticoids, isotretinoin, antipsychotics, beta-blockers, thiazides, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, pregnancy
Keep or stop when TG normalizes?
Repeat TG 4–12 weeks after changes; fasting for TG-focused evaluation

d3uwqr0b.sub: Two different problems: moderate HTG (150–499) is an ASCVD risk marker treated through LDL/apoB and lifestyle; severe HTG (≥500, especially ≥1000) is a pancreatitis risk treated urgently and specifically.

74nwgyvb.name: Chylomicrons versus VLDL

rows.t: Only when LPL clearance is overwhelmed or deficient (TG usually >1000)
Large chylomicrons: low; their remnants: yes
Dietary fat restriction, LPL function (insulin, fibrates modestly), apoC-III lowering
Carbohydrate/alcohol restriction, weight, fibrates, omega-3, insulin sensitization

74nwgyvb.sub: Both carry TG; the lipoprotein tells you the mechanism and the treatment. (Routed from your sticky-note question.)

wjcp3ygs.name: Diet for severe hypertriglyceridemia

rows.t: <10–15% of energy (often <20–30 g/day) until TG <1000; FCS: lifelong
Chylomicron production is proportional to fat intake
Blocks TG clearance; potent VLDL stimulus
Absorbed via portal vein, not chylomicrons

wjcp3ygs.sub: The only intervention that works within days. (Routed from "severe high TG best diet".)

9y9yxmia.name: HTG-induced acute pancreatitis

rows.t: Lipase, TG on admission (TG falls quickly with fasting, so measure early), exclude gallstones/alcohol

Hypokalemia is the main hazard of the protocol
Consider if TG >1000 with organ failure, severe pancreatitis, or pregnancy; evidence observational
Fibrate + omega-3, very-low-fat diet, treat diabetes/alcohol, stop offending drugs; lipid clinic follow-up

9y9yxmia.sub: TG >1000 at presentation, no other cause. Lower TG fast; insulin infusion is the workhorse. (Routed from "IV dextrose and insulin and potassium".)

rows.t: Was benefit explained by TG lowering?

REDUCE-IT secondary analyses; EVAPORATE plaque regression
If TG falls below 150 on therapy, stop?
No clear basis to stop if the original indication (ASCVD or diabetes + risk factors with TG 135–499) stands
Trial continued regardless of on-treatment TG
If TG improved because of lifestyle/diabetes control before starting?
TG <135 at baseline was not studied; indication weaker
Judgment: treat remaining residual risk, not the number
AF ↑ (5.3% vs 3.9%), bleeding ↑ slightly; mineral-oil placebo controversy (STRENGTH neutral with corn oil)

Statin from age 8–10 for HeFH with LDL ≥190, or ≥160 with risk factors

Pravastatin/fluvastatin with cyclosporine; low-dose rosuva/atorva otherwise

Pitavastatin or pravastatin; atorva/rosuva low dose with monitoring

Same thresholds; transdermal estrogen if HT needed with HTG

Treat by CV risk as usual

Risk elevated; same thresholds by age/duration

ny2q6mf8.name: Monitoring and follow-up

4–12 weeks after starting or changing therapy
Confirms response and adherence; dose titration
Response <expected → adherence, absorption, interactions; then add ezetimibe
Not required after baseline unless symptoms
Maximal tolerated statin, ezetimibe trial, LDL values, diagnosis (ASCVD/FH), intolerance details
Weight, BP, glucose/A1c, smoking, risk recalculation if untreated
Every 5–10 years if CAC 0 and untreated
Power of zero has a half-life

r1t6990j.sub: Evidence layer. One row per guideline or trial; link cells elsewhere to these rows. No URLs here — verify at the journal or society site.

jlrfw8n4.name: Clinical logic: how reasoning works

rows.t: What exactly is the problem, in one sentence?
A good representation retrieves the right illness scripts; a poor one retrieves everything
Which stored pattern does this match?
Most diagnoses are made this way in seconds; the failures are anchoring and premature closure
How likely is it, and what would a test change?
Converts clinical impressions into decisions about testing and treating
Testing layers; triggers for secondary-cause screens
What mechanism produces this, and what else must then be true?
Generates hypotheses and refutable predictions; explains atypical features
How could I be wrong here?
Most diagnostic error is cognitive, not knowledge; structure beats vigilance
How much should this evidence move me?
Separates guideline strength from certainty; converts trial effects into the patient's absolute gain
What does this patient want, knowing the real numbers?
A probability becomes a decision only through values; nocebo and adherence are design problems
How will I find out if I am wrong?
Turns uncertainty into a plan with a review point and a definition of failure

jlrfw8n4.sub: The engine beneath every disease node. Each domain is a way a clinician gets from a story to a decision, with the places it breaks and the fix. Disease nodes should → link to these tables rather than restate them.

8c5d69cm.name: Problem representation

rows.t: Age, sex, relevant background (pregnancy, immunosuppression, CKD)
Base rates change with the host
Ignoring the host: "chest pain" means different things at 25 and 75
Acute / subacute / chronic; progressive, relapsing, stable
Tempo narrows the differential more than any single symptom
Treating a 10-year symptom as an emergency, or a 10-hour one as chronic
"Episodic palpitations with diaphoresis and headache" rather than a list
Qualifiers (episodic vs constant, unilateral vs bilateral) map to illness scripts
Raw symptom lists that match everything
What makes it better or worse; context (post-prandial, nocturnal, exertional)
Defines the edges of the pattern

8c5d69cm.sub: The one-sentence summary that turns a story into a searchable pattern: who, time course, key syndrome, key modifiers. Get this right and the differential writes itself.

vfl294yj.name: Worked example: problem representation

rows.t: 55-year-old woman with fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation
A list; could be depression, thyroid, anaemia, sleep…
55-year-old woman with 6 months of progressive fatigue and 8 kg weight gain, cold intolerance and constipation, 2 years after radioiodine for Graves disease
Illness script for post-ablative hypothyroidism; TSH is the test; competitors listed by what does not fit
One sentence; time course first; include the modifier that points at mechanism
Transfer to notes, handoffs and the differential

vfl294yj.sub: Same facts, two summaries. The second is searchable.

pcg5aqrm.name: Illness scripts (System 1)

rows.t: Who gets it: age, exposures, risks
Base-rate aware when scripts are well formed
Scripts formed on atypical training cases
Acting before the match is checked
Typical presentation, experienced domain, low stakes, time pressure
Atypical presentation, high stakes, unfamiliar domain, fatigue
The diagnostic time-out is the deliberate brake

pcg5aqrm.sub: Fast, automatic matching of the representation to stored patterns. Powerful and mostly right; the errors are predictable.

zzp14xn6.name: Probabilistic reasoning (Bayes in the clinic)

rows.t: Decide test vs treat vs observe
Testing when it cannot change management
Ignoring prevalence when interpreting a result
A positive screen for a rare disease is usually a false positive
Test performance measured in sicker patients than yours
Series raises specificity; parallel raises sensitivity
Screen → confirm (ARR → saline load); rule-out panels in emergencies
Confirming with a correlated test adds little

zzp14xn6.sub: Every test moves a probability from pretest to post-test. The decision depends on where the post-test lands relative to thresholds, not on whether the result was "positive".

k9tr3caa.name: Pretest probability

rows.t: Wells, HEART, FRAX, Dutch Lipid Clinic score, ARR triggers
Use within the population it was derived in
Primary aldosteronism ~5–10% of hypertension, ~20% of resistant
Hypokalemia + resistant HTN raises aldosteronism well above 10%
Avoid double counting the same clue
Calibrate against outcomes; gestalt drifts high after a miss

k9tr3caa.sub: Where the reasoning starts. Sources in order of quality: validated rule, local prevalence, published prevalence in similar patients, gestalt.

ng2swd1p.name: Likelihood ratios

rows.t: Shifts ~45 percentage points from a mid-range pretest
The test was not worth doing
Preparation changes the LR; see HTN node
Pretest odds × LR = post-test odds (odds = p/(1−p))
Fagan nomogram or a mental 15/30/45 shortcut

ng2swd1p.sub: How much a result moves the odds. LR+ = sensitivity / (1 − specificity); LR− = (1 − sensitivity) / specificity.

hay2wzku.name: Test and treatment thresholds

rows.t: Harm of testing vs harm of missing; cost; the test's LR
Lp(a) once in everyone: test threshold ≈ 0 because the test is cheap, harmless and the result is permanent
Benefit of treatment vs harm/cost of treating the untreated
Statin at 7.5% 10-year risk: low harm, modest absolute benefit; CAC used when the probability sits near the line
Severity of the disease, reversibility, patient values
Pheochromocytoma: low test threshold because the miss is catastrophic
Thresholds get forgotten once a label is attached
Re-derive the probability when a new clinician inherits the case

hay2wzku.sub: Two lines on the probability axis decide what to do. Below the test threshold: do nothing. Between: test. Above the treatment threshold: treat without testing.

dqbzphdj.name: Causal and mechanistic reasoning

rows.t: Ask what mechanism produces each qualifier
Postural headache after lumbar puncture → CSF leak
A plausible mechanism is not evidence it occurred
If mechanism X, then Y should also be present
Primary aldosteronism → suppressed renin should accompany the raised aldosterone
Confirmation bias: look for what would refute
Occam (one explanation) vs Hickam (patients can have several)
Older patients: multiple; young with multisystem findings: look for one
Ask what else could produce this picture
Hypothyroidism raising LDL; drugs raising BP
Watchful waiting with a defined endpoint
Only when the miss is recoverable
Bone: fracture = fragility × load; HTN: resistance = measurement × adherence × secondary cause
Linear thinking in a looped system

dqbzphdj.sub: Pathophysiology explains why the pattern looks the way it does and predicts what else must be true. Used to generate hypotheses and to check them, not as proof.

poiju43f.name: Metacognition and cognitive error

rows.t: First impression dominates despite new data
Re-derive the representation when data conflict
Stopping the search once one answer fits
Ask "what else?" before closing; name the second diagnosis
Osteoporosis treated without the secondary-cause screen
Recent or vivid cases inflate probability
Over-testing for the disease missed last month
Seeking data that supports the favourite
Ordering only the test expected to be positive
Ask how the disease presents at the extremes of age
Decisions degrade with fatigue and emotion
Before any new label or irreversible treatment

poiju43f.sub: Knowing when System 1 cannot be trusted. The remedy is structural (time-outs, checklists, forced alternatives), not willpower.

ya3gwkte.name: Diagnostic time-out

rows.t: What is the problem representation in one sentence?
What is the leading diagnosis and what does not fit?
What is the must-not-miss alternative, and have I excluded it?
Is this label inherited, and did anyone verify it?
If I am wrong, how will I find out, and when?

ya3gwkte.sub: A 60-second structured pause before committing. Use at the moment of labelling, before an irreversible step, and at handoffs.

iaflgs01.name: Evidence appraisal

rows.t: Systematic review of RCTs > RCT > cohort > case-control > series > opinion
Start with the best available; a good cohort beats a poor RCT
High / moderate / low / very low after risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias
Read the certainty, not just the recommendation strength
LDL, BMD, A1c vs MI, fracture, death
Surrogates are fine when the drug class has outcome proof; new classes need outcomes
Niacin, torcetrapib, pemafibrate: surrogate moved, outcomes did not
Hypothesis-generating unless pre-specified with interaction test
ACCORD-Lipid TG/HDL subgroup → PROMINENT tested it: negative
Would this patient have been enrolled?
Look for registry and observational signals
Assuming absence of evidence is evidence of absence

iaflgs01.sub: How much weight a source deserves, and how to translate relative effects into what this patient gains.

mpms801y.name: Absolute vs relative effects

rows.t: 23 vs 91 over 10 years for the same drug
Compare with NNT for the trade-off
Quote ARR and NNT to patients and to yourself

mpms801y.sub: Relative risk reduction is constant across baseline risk; absolute benefit is not. Decisions run on absolute numbers.

br9720kt.name: Decision-making with the patient

rows.t: "Of 100 people like you, X helped, Y harmed, Z unchanged"
Relative risk or vague "it lowers your risk"
Function, longevity, pill burden, cost, fear of specific outcomes
Preference-sensitive decisions (statin at borderline risk, anabolic vs antiresorptive)
Improves knowledge and accuracy of expectations
Frame side effects proportionally; SAMSON data
"This drug causes muscle pain" as the opening line
Simplify, align with routine, address cost first
Half of statin users stop within a year
What to watch for, when to return, how to reach us
Why this, why not that, what would change it
Future clinicians inherit reasoning, not just a label

br9720kt.sub: The last step is not a calculation. Values, goals, burden and trust decide what a probability becomes.

rtjufddo.name: Working with uncertainty

rows.t: "Most likely X; Y not excluded; we will know by Z"
Date and parameter that triggers re-evaluation
Lipids at 4–12 weeks; BP log at 2 weeks; DXA at 2 years
What result means the plan is wrong
LDL reduction <30% = adherence/absorption check, not "statin failure"
Failure returns to history, adherence, secondary causes
Keep a personal list of surprises
Where the disease nodes loop back
Every node's "treatment failure" row should → link here
The engine is the common denominator

rtjufddo.sub: Diagnosis is iterative. Design the follow-up so that being wrong is discovered early and cheaply.

46njzig6.name: Sources

rows.t: Kassirer, Wong, Kopelman — Learning Clinical Reasoning (2nd ed.)
Problem representation, hypothesis generation, Bayesian reasoning, thresholds
Pauker & Kassirer, NEJM 1980 — The threshold approach to clinical decision making
Croskerry, Academic Medicine 2003 and later — cognitive biases, dual-process model, debiasing
Bowen, NEJM 2006 — Educational strategies to promote clinical diagnostic reasoning
Problem representation, illness scripts, semantic qualifiers
Guyatt et al. — Users' Guides to the Medical Literature (JAMA/McGraw-Hill); GRADE Working Group
National Academies 2015 — Improving Diagnosis in Health Care
Diagnostic error as a system problem
Elwyn et al., BMJ 2017 — three-talk model of shared decision making
Cabrera & Cabrera — Systems Thinking Made Simple (DSRP)

46njzig6.sub: Foundations for the reasoning layer. Verify editions and details at the source.

j5znz8rf.name: Hypertension: evaluation

rows.t: How did it start, what might be causing it, what has it done, and what has been tried?
Onset, symptoms of a secondary cause, pregnancy and family history, drugs and lifestyle, treatment history
Is this an emergency, a dangerous cause, or a drug that becomes dangerous?
Hypertensive emergency, dissection, pheochromocytoma (never beta-block first), thyrotoxic heart failure, preeclampsia, hypokalaemia, young onset, bilateral RAS
Does the examination show a cause or damage?
Correct measurement first; then habitus, fundi, pulses, bruits, heart, thyroid, skin
Office reading or sustained out-of-office hypertension?
White-coat and masked hypertension are common and managed differently
Is there a cause we can remove?
5–15% have a secondary cause; aldosteronism alone is 5–10% and curable
What do we need before treating?
Detects damage, secondary causes and drug-choice constraints
Treatment threshold and BP target depend on stage and ASCVD risk
Damage raises risk and redirects drug choice
What has been tried, and is it really resistant?
Pseudo-resistance is common; true resistance signals a secondary cause

j5znz8rf.sub: Spine order shared by every disease-state project: History · Red flags · Examination · Diagnosis · Exclusions · Testing · then domain-specific rows · Sources. Red cells are never-miss prompts.

22f7jfg1.name: Confirming the diagnosis

rows.t: Prior readings, pregnancy BP, childhood BP

22f7jfg1.sub: A single office reading diagnoses nothing. Out-of-office measurement separates sustained, white-coat and masked hypertension, which carry different risks and different treatment.

iw4yv8qe.name: Office measurement technique

rows.t: Bladder 80% of arm circumference; large cuff for arm ≥32 cm
Back supported, feet flat, arm at heart level
No caffeine, smoking, exercise 30 min before; empty bladder
≥2 readings 1 min apart, average; both arms first visit

iw4yv8qe.sub: Most "resistant" or "labile" hypertension is measurement error. Each item below moves the reading 5–15 mmHg.

qlazyzvb.name: Home blood pressure monitoring

rows.t: Validated upper-arm cuff, patient brings it in to compare
2 readings morning and 2 evening, 7 days; discard day 1; average
Diagnosis, white-coat vs masked, titration, adherence check

qlazyzvb.sub: Preferred confirmation when ABPM is unavailable; also the backbone of titration.

sh03zixl.name: Ambulatory monitoring thresholds

rows.t: Night fall <10% = non-dipper; reverse dipper if night > day
Non-dipping: OSA, CKD, autonomic failure, secondary causes
Treat as hypertension; common in diabetes, CKD, smokers

sh03zixl.sub: Reference standard. Night-time BP and dipping status predict events better than office readings.

b6ax7mnf.name: Staging and risk

rows.t: Drug therapy if ASCVD ≥10%, diabetes, CKD, or clinical CVD; otherwise lifestyle
Drug therapy (often two agents) plus lifestyle
Emergency: admit; urgency: oral therapy, close follow-up

b6ax7mnf.sub: Treatment threshold and target depend on stage plus 10-year ASCVD risk and comorbidity, not on the number alone.

39rr2iui.name: ASCVD risk inputs (pooled cohort / PREVENT)

rows.t: PREVENT drops race, adds eGFR, BMI, UACR, social index
CKD, inflammatory disease, South Asian ancestry, metabolic syndrome

39rr2iui.sub: Gather every input in the history so the calculator can be run in the room.

2etad426.name: Secondary hypertension

rows.t: Resistant HTN, hypokalemia, incidentaloma, OSA, family history
Bruit, creatinine rise on ACEi/ARB, flash pulmonary oedema
Paroxysms, labile BP, incidentaloma, family history
Snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime sleepiness, neck >17/16 in, non-dipping on ABPM
STOP-BANG; polysomnography or home sleep test
CPAP lowers BP modestly; biggest effect in resistant HTN
Weight gain, striae, bruising, proximal weakness, steroid exposure
1 mg overnight DST, late-night salivary cortisol, 24-h UFC
Young; arm–leg BP gradient; delayed femoral pulses; rib notching
Early onset, family history, hypokalemia with low aldosterone and low renin
Specific therapies (amiloride for Liddle; dexamethasone for GRA)

2etad426.sub: Screen when the history says so, not in everyone. The triggers in the first row decide who gets the workup below.

kxecsf93.name: Triggers for a secondary-cause workup

rows.t: Onset <30 years, or >55 with abrupt onset
Essential hypertension is unusual at the extremes
Resistant hypertension (≥3 drugs incl. diuretic, or ≥4 to control)
OSA is the commonest secondary cause
Abrupt rise in a previously controlled patient
Flash pulmonary oedema, abdominal bruit, renal asymmetry, rise in creatinine on ACEi/ARB
Family history of early hypertension or stroke <40

kxecsf93.sub: Any one trigger justifies at least an aldosterone–renin screen; several justify the full panel.

7yvqat78.name: Primary aldosteronism workup

rows.t: Plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC) and plasma renin activity (PRA) or direct renin
Positive: PAC >10 ng/dL with suppressed renin (PRA <1 ng/mL/h); ARR >30 (PAC/PRA) supports; PAC >20 with suppressed renin and hypokalemia is near-diagnostic
Oral sodium loading (24-h urine aldosterone >12 mcg), saline infusion (PAC >10 ng/dL post), captopril, or fludrocortisone test
Skip confirmation if spontaneous hypokalemia + undetectable renin + PAC >20
Adrenal CT; adrenal venous sampling if surgery is wanted and age >35
CT misses small adenomas and over-calls incidentalomas; AVS lateralization decides surgery
Unilateral: adrenalectomy. Bilateral or not operable: spironolactone or eplerenone
Target renin unsuppressed on MRA; aldosterone excess harms the heart independent of BP

7yvqat78.sub: The most common curable cause (5–10% of all hypertension; ~20% of resistant). Screening is cheap; the sequence matters.

ikm6sjdk.name: Conditions for a valid aldosterone–renin ratio

rows.t: Mid-morning, seated 5–15 min after ≥2 h upright
Interfering drugs: stop 4–6 weeks if feasible
Interfering drugs: stop 2 weeks if feasible
ACEi, ARB, DRIs, dihydropyridine CCBs, beta-blockers
ACEi/ARB raise renin; beta-blockers suppress renin (false positive)
Use to keep BP controlled during testing
Interpret with caution: a suppressed renin on ACEi/ARB is still strongly suggestive
Document the drugs on the requisition

ikm6sjdk.sub: Most false results come from potassium, posture and drugs. Note the morning sample taken seated after being upright ≥2 h.

fzd6as8q.name: Renovascular hypertension

rows.t: Young woman, no family history, bruit
Older, diffuse atherosclerosis, CKD, flash pulmonary oedema
CORAL/ASTRAL: stenting rarely beats medical therapy
Suggests bilateral stenosis or solitary kidney

fzd6as8q.sub: Two diseases: fibromuscular dysplasia (young women; treatable with angioplasty) and atherosclerotic stenosis (older; medical therapy usually equals stenting).

9lydb7o9.name: Pheochromocytoma workup

rows.t: Plasma free metanephrines (supine, after 30 min rest) or 24-h urine fractionated metanephrines
TCAs, SNRIs, levodopa, sympathomimetics, acute illness, caffeine; sampling upright
Mild elevation (<2× ULN) usually false positive; repeat under ideal conditions
CT abdomen/pelvis; MRI; functional imaging (Ga-DOTATATE, MIBG) if negative
Do not image first: incidentalomas mislead
Offer to all: SDHx, VHL, RET, NF1, etc.
Alpha-blockade (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) ≥7–14 days, then beta-blocker if needed, volume expansion

9lydb7o9.sub: Rare but dangerous; screen generously when the story fits, confirm carefully because false positives are common.

hnjrycft.name: Target organ damage

rows.t: ECG (LVH), prior MI, heart failure, AF; echo if ECG abnormal
Claudication, bruits, erectile dysfunction, ankle-brachial index
Abdominal aorta exam/ultrasound in men >65 who smoked

hnjrycft.sub: Present damage moves the patient to a higher-risk group and changes drug choice.

29om6n2d.name: Drug- and substance-induced hypertension

rows.t: Stop or minimize; acetaminophen also raises BP modestly
Stop; avoid beta-blocker alone with cocaine
Herbal: ephedra, ma huang, yohimbine, St John's wort (interactions)

29om6n2d.sub: Review everything taken, including over-the-counter, herbal and recreational. Stopping the cause often beats adding a fourth drug.

fhcxd5e2.name: Lifestyle contributors

rows.t: Processed foods, restaurant meals, added salt; 24-h urine sodium if unsure
Aerobic and resistance; minutes per week

fhcxd5e2.sub: Quantified, each is worth roughly one drug; together they can be worth more.

bzem77ji.name: Baseline laboratory and other tests

rows.t: Basic metabolic panel (Na, K, Cr/eGFR, Ca, glucose)
Echo if abnormal or HF symptoms
Metanephrines, cortisol testing, sleep study, renal imaging

bzem77ji.sub: A fixed minimum panel for everyone; add-ons follow the triggers in layer 3.

m40a0bda.name: Treatment history and resistant hypertension

rows.t: Drug, dose, duration, why stopped, side effects
Previous intolerance narrows options; many stop silently
Uncontrolled on 3 drugs incl. diuretic at optimal doses, or controlled on ≥4
Spironolactone 25–50 mg (check K, eGFR) → amiloride, beta-blocker, doxazosin, hydralazine, minoxidil
Resistance is a trigger, not a label

m40a0bda.sub: Before calling it resistant: confirm the readings, the adherence and the doses. True resistance is a secondary-cause trigger.

9sdtdska.name: Excluding pseudo-resistance

rows.t: Pharmacy refill data, pill counts, directly observed dosing, urine drug assay where available
Simplify to once-daily single-pill combinations; address cost, side effects, beliefs
Doses below maximum; no diuretic or wrong diuretic for eGFR; duplicate classes
Optimize: RAS blocker + CCB + thiazide-like (chlorthalidone/indapamide) at full doses

9sdtdska.sub: Most apparent resistance is one of these four.

zerjqkpc.name: Osteoporosis: clinical history

rows.t: What has happened, what is inherited, what has been tried, and how does she live?
Fracture history and FRAX inputs set the tier; medications, falls, nutrition and prior treatment set the plan
Is there anything rare, deadly or disabling hiding behind "osteoporosis"?
Myeloma, metastases, hypophosphatasia, AFF prodrome, denosumab rebound, hypocalcaemia before antiresorptives, ONJ, cord compression — each has a specific step that routine care skips
Are the signs of vertebral fracture, falls risk or a secondary cause present?
Height loss and kyphosis find silent fractures; gait and strength predict the next fall; Cushingoid, OI and osteomalacia signs redirect the workup
Does she meet criteria, and how high is the risk?
BMD or fracture makes the diagnosis; the category (high vs very high) decides anabolic-first vs antiresorptive-first
Is something else driving bone loss?
One-third of women and half of men have a contributor; the history points at which one, the labs confirm it
What do we measure, when, and what does each result change?
DXA and VFA define the category; the lab screen finds the contributor; BTMs follow adherence
One row per guideline or statement

zerjqkpc.sub: Spine order shared by every disease-state project: History · Red flags · Examination · Diagnosis · Exclusions · Testing · then domain-specific rows · Sources. Red cells are never-miss prompts.

mme2iou9.name: Fracture history

rows.t: "Have you broken any bone as an adult? How did it happen?"
Low-trauma = fall from standing height or less. Excludes fingers, toes, face, skull.
Record site, age, mechanism; treat as fragility unless clearly high-energy
Often silent; one morphometric fracture reclassifies the patient
Highest mortality; indicates very high risk
Treat without waiting for DXA; anabolic-first discussion
Other sites: wrist, humerus, pelvis, ribs
Distal forearm fracture in 50s is often the first warning
Assess, do not dismiss as "just a fall"

mme2iou9.sub: A prior fragility fracture is the strongest single predictor of the next one and, at hip or spine, usually makes the diagnosis regardless of T-score.

hwwdp6cv.name: Vertebral fracture

rows.t: Measured stadiometer height vs. recalled peak adult height
≥4 cm historical, or ≥2 cm prospectively measured
Order VFA or lateral thoracolumbar radiograph
Sudden mid/low back pain with bending, lifting, coughing; eased lying flat
Any episode lasting weeks, especially with no clear injury
Image; one morphometric fracture changes the diagnosis and the treatment tier
Document grade and level; count the number of fractures (multiplicity raises risk)

hwwdp6cv.sub: Two-thirds are clinically silent. You find them by asking about height and back pain and by looking (VFA or lateral spine film), not by waiting for them to be reported.

d6lmpr8g.name: Genant semiquantitative grading

rows.t: Distinguish from Scheuermann, degenerative wedging, Schmorl nodes
Often symptomatic; consider referral if neurological signs

d6lmpr8g.sub: Used to decide whether a vertebral deformity counts as a fracture. Grade 1 is where most disagreement lives.

yllu5ge5.name: Family history

rows.t: Hip fracture at any age? Other fractures, "dowager hump", height loss?
Heritable component of bone strength and microarchitecture
Raises suspicion of monogenic causes if young
Not a FRAX input; note it

yllu5ge5.sub: Parental hip fracture is a FRAX input independent of BMD.

pe6q65k4.name: FRAX inputs and other risk factors

rows.t: Risk roughly doubles each decade after 50
Low BMI (<20) is a risk; weight loss is a separate flag
≥5 mg prednisone-equivalent for ≥3 months, ever or current
Any cause from the Secondary causes layer
FRAX ignores it once femoral neck BMD is entered
Argue for treating at lower threshold

pe6q65k4.sub: Collect every FRAX field in the history so the 10-year probability can be run with or without BMD. Then ask about the risks FRAX does not capture.

k3ntvtlb.name: Risks FRAX does not capture

rows.t: Lumbar spine T-score much lower than femoral neck
Fractures at higher BMD; TBS lower
Use TBS adjustment or treat as RA in FRAX
Risk scales with number and severity

k3ntvtlb.sub: Clinical judgement adjusts the number. Each of these argues for treating at a lower FRAX threshold.

b30gh3v0.name: Secondary causes

rows.t: Hyperparathyroidism, thyroid, hypogonadism, Cushing, diabetes, vitamin D
Ca, PTH, TSH, 25-OH D, sex steroids
Celiac, bariatric surgery, IBD, liver disease
CKD-MBD changes agent choice: avoid bisphosphonates below eGFR 30–35
Blue sclerae, hypermobility, dentinogenesis imperfecta, childhood fractures
Consider OI, Ehlers-Danlos; genetics referral if young with multiple fractures
Stroke, Parkinson, MS, spinal cord injury
Tick each test as it results
The gate before treatment: nothing starts until tier 1 is back

b30gh3v0.sub: Up to a third of women and half of men with osteoporosis have a contributing cause. The history points at which one; the labs confirm it.

6vgpsyk5.name: Endocrine causes

rows.t: Stones, bone pain, fatigue, "high calcium once"
Ca, PTH, 25-OH D, 24-h urine Ca, eGFR
Normalize TSH; avoid TSH <0.1 unless thyroid cancer suppression
Address cause; bone agent still usually needed
Weight gain, bruising, proximal weakness, any steroid exposure
Steroid-induced bone loss is fast and partly reversible
BMD underestimates risk; avoid TZDs; consider SGLT2 fracture signal (canagliflozin)
Bone pain, proximal weakness, low sun, malabsorption
Replete before antiresorptives (hypocalcemia risk with denosumab/zoledronate)

6vgpsyk5.sub: The ones an endocrinologist is expected not to miss.

r3vo930j.name: Primary hyperparathyroidism: workup

rows.t: High/high-normal Ca with non-suppressed PTH = PHPT
Replete before judging PTH; deficiency raises PTH
Excludes FHH (Ca/Cr clearance ratio <0.01); informs surgical criteria
T ≤ −2.5 at any site is a surgical indication

r3vo930j.sub: Classic bone pattern: cortical (distal radius) loss out of proportion to spine.

o1u2skvt.name: Thyroid excess: workup

rows.t: If on levothyroxine: dose, adherence, timing, interacting drugs
Over-replacement is the commonest cause; reduce dose unless cancer suppression is intended
Recheck 12–24 months after euthyroid; often partly recovers

o1u2skvt.sub: Suppressed TSH from any source (endogenous or levothyroxine) raises turnover and lowers BMD.

rcav4ots.name: Hypogonadism

rows.t: Age at menopause (<45 = early; <40 = POI); oophorectomy; amenorrhea >1 yr before menopause; aromatase inhibitor
Libido, erectile function, testes size, androgen deprivation therapy
Treat the cause; testosterone alone is not an osteoporosis drug
Prolactinoma, anorexia nervosa, athletic amenorrhea, opioid use

rcav4ots.sub: Sex steroid deficiency is the dominant mechanism in both sexes; timing and duration matter.

qby8q7tm.name: Cushing syndrome: workup

rows.t: Cortisol >1.8 µg/dL = abnormal; check estrogen use (CBG)
Suppressed = adrenal; normal/high = pituitary or ectopic
Adrenal CT or pituitary MRI; endocrine referral

qby8q7tm.sub: Exclude exogenous steroids first (oral, inhaled, topical, intra-articular, "supplements"). Two abnormal first-line tests before imaging.

p5nm7gsg.name: Vitamin D deficiency and osteomalacia: workup

rows.t: <20 ng/mL deficient; <12 severe; target ≥30 before denosumab/zoledronate
Low Ca/PO4, high ALP, high PTH = osteomalacia pattern
If phosphate low with normal D: FGF23, TmP/GFR
Replete (D3 50,000 IU weekly ×8 or 1,000–4,000 IU daily) and recheck 3 months
Re-evaluate BMD after repletion before labelling osteoporosis

p5nm7gsg.sub: Low 25-OH D with high ALP, low phosphate or bone pain is osteomalacia until shown otherwise; replete before any antiresorptive.

mefilbe2.name: Hypercalciuria: workup

rows.t: Exclude PHPT and vitamin D excess
Salt drives calciuria; stone risk profile
Sodium <2.3 g/day, fluids; thiazide or chlorthalidone; potassium citrate if hypocitraturic; recheck 24-h urine

mefilbe2.sub: A stone former with low BMD usually has idiopathic hypercalciuria; it responds to thiazide and sodium restriction.

r6nzbkuq.name: GI and malabsorptive causes

rows.t: Bloating, iron deficiency, diarrhea, family history; can be silent
Ca, 25-OH D, PTH; DXA; consider spine imaging
Oral bisphosphonates poorly absorbed; use IV or denosumab

r6nzbkuq.sub: Ask about the gut in everyone with low BMD and no obvious reason, and in anyone with low calcium or vitamin D despite supplements.

36fhmf6u.name: Celiac disease: workup

rows.t: tTG-IgA + total IgA (on a gluten-containing diet)
tTG-IgA >10× ULN strongly positive; total IgA excludes IgA deficiency
If IgA deficient: DGP-IgG or tTG-IgG
Negative result excludes; useful if already gluten-free
Nutritional panel: iron, ferritin, folate, B12, 25-OH D, calcium, zinc
DXA at diagnosis; repeat 1–2 years on gluten-free diet
BMD often improves; treat if still osteoporotic

36fhmf6u.sub: Test while still eating gluten. Silent celiac is common in unexplained low BMD and in low calcium or vitamin D despite supplements.

80uwedco.name: Post-bariatric bone: workup

rows.t: Procedure type and year; weight trajectory; supplements and adherence
Spine and hip; consider annually early
Calcium citrate 1,200–1,500 mg/day in divided doses; D3 to 25-OH D ≥30; protein ≥60–80 g/day; IV zoledronate or denosumab if indicated (correct Ca/D first)

80uwedco.sub: Malabsorptive procedures (RYGB, BPD-DS) cause calcium/vitamin D malabsorption, secondary hyperparathyroidism and rapid loss; oral bisphosphonates are poorly absorbed.

x5p13xad.name: Hematologic and oncologic causes

Imaging: whole-body low-dose CT or MRI (skeletal survey insensitive)

bnkskvhx.name: Bone turnover markers (BTM)

rows.t: Serum β-CTX (resorption) and intact/total P1NP (formation). These are the IOF/IFCC reference markers; others (NTX, osteocalcin, bone ALP, TRACP5b) are second line.
Use one lab and one assay for serial values; automated CTX assays differ by platform.
CTX: fasting, morning (07–10h), same time each visit; food lowers CTX ~20% and there is a circadian nadir in the afternoon. P1NP is not meaningfully affected by food or time of day.
CTX accumulates in CKD (eGFR <30) and is raised for 6–12 months after any fracture. P1NP is falsely low on glucocorticoids and rises after fracture too.

Draw CTX + P1NP at the pre-treatment visit, with the secondary-cause screen. Very high values prompt a second look at secondary causes (hyperparathyroidism, thyroid excess, Paget, metastases, osteomalacia) before treating.
A single baseline is not a fracture predictor for the individual; the association with fracture risk is modest and population-level.

Repeat CTX (and P1NP) 3 months after oral bisphosphonate, 3–6 months after IV or denosumab. Expected: CTX falls ≥ the least significant change (~30%, assay-dependent) or into the lower half of the premenopausal reference range; P1NP falls ≥ ~20–25%.

A fall below LSC = non-response gate → check adherence, dosing technique (fasting, water, upright 30 min), absorption (celiac, bariatric, PPI), and hidden secondary causes before switching agents (TRIO study).
P1NP at 1–3 months: rise > 10 µg/L (teriparatide) above baseline confirms biological response; romosozumab gives an early P1NP rise and CTX fall.
Patients already on a bisphosphonate blunt the rise; interpret against their own baseline, not the reference range.
CTX every 1–2 years off drug. Rising back above the premenopausal median (or above the patient's own pre-treatment value) is a trigger to re-assess with DXA and consider restarting.
Evidence for marker-guided restart is observational; combine with DXA change and new fractures rather than CTX alone.

CTX rebounds above baseline within 3–6 months of a missed dose. Use CTX at ~6 months after the last dose to time and judge the follow-on bisphosphonate (zoledronate when CTX rises; repeat if still high).
Stopping denosumab without a bisphosphonate risks rebound vertebral fractures; CTX is the practical marker for this transition logic.
Diagnosis of osteoporosis; selecting a first agent; replacing DXA; deciding treatment in CKD stage 4–5 or shortly after fracture.
Report the specific marker, assay and sampling conditions in the note so later values are comparable.

☐ Baseline drawn fasting a.m. before drug → ☐ 3–6 month value drawn same conditions → ☐ change ≥ LSC? Yes: continue, next DXA at 1–2 y. No: adherence/absorption/secondary-cause review before any switch.
Checkboxes are the logic gate; each clear answer closes a branch.
Open for the literature list with DOIs.
Add your own in the reference table; cross-link from any cell with ↳.

bnkskvhx.sub: Prompt: are we measuring to decide, or to feel better? BTMs monitor response and adherence; they do not diagnose osteoporosis or replace DXA. Reference markers: serum β-CTX (resorption) and P1NP (formation).

fhzdcdor.name: PMOS: decision support

rows.t: What is the cycle, androgen, weight and reproductive story — and what has been tried?

Oligo-ovulation and hyperandrogenism are two of the three criteria and both are largely history; tempo of androgen symptoms separates PMOS from tumor; medication review explains much "weight-loss resistance"
Is there anything that stops routine PMOS care and sends her to urgent evaluation?
Virilization, rapid progression and very high testosterone are not PMOS until proven; safety red flags (pregnancy, self-harm, purging, PMB) change the pathway before any diagnosis
Tumor workup, pregnancy test, behavioral health, endometrial evaluation
Are the signs of androgen excess, insulin resistance or a mimic present?
mFG by region makes clinical hyperandrogenism countable; acanthosis and waist mark the metabolic axis; Cushingoid discriminators and virilization redirect the workup
Does she meet criteria for her stage of life, after exclusions?
Two of three (HA, OD, PCOM) in adults; adolescents need HA + OD with no AMH/US; after menopause there is no Rotterdam — recognize from history. Phenotype letter plus a metabolic axis drives the plan
Adolescent rule, postmenopausal rule, phenotype A–D
PMOS is a diagnosis of exclusion: pregnancy, thyroid, prolactin, NCCAH, Cushing, severe IR syndromes, FHA and POI each have a specific test and a specific treatment
What do we measure, how, and when?
Assay and timing decide the answer: LC-MS/MS testosterone against the lab's own ULN, calculated free T, off CHC ≥3 months, AM follicular 17-OHP; OGTT over A1c; insulin not for diagnosis
Core panel, androgen chain, AMH rules, glycemia, liver
What are the loops we are trying to calm?

Insulin → ovarian androgen and low SHBG; androgen → follicular arrest and visceral fat → more IR; rapid GnRH pulses → LH over FSH. Calming any loop eases the others — this is why insulin-targeted therapy fixes cycles
Explains Domain 10 drug choice; patient primer
Separate from the diagnostic phenotype: what actually needs treating?
Six axes (glycemia, adiposity, cardiovascular, liver, reproductive safety, symptom burden) each with a status, so the plan is written against problems rather than the label
Feeds Domain 9 clusters and Domain 12 monitoring
Which cluster is she in, and what is the reasoning path?
Weight-loss resistance, irregular cycles/endometrial protection, hirsutism, fatigue, mood/eating, fertility — each with ask / measure / act and an escalation ladder
Cluster scores from intake; goal match
Before each prescription: who it suits, what rules it out, what to check, how to titrate, when to review
CHC eligibility (US MEC), spironolactone needs contraception, metformin eGFR floor, GLP-1/tirzepatide pregnancy washout and the tirzepatide oral-OC rule, letrozole for fertility only
Does the condition still shape her risk after the reproductive years?

No new Rotterdam diagnosis; androgens stay relatively higher; risk calculators do not include PMOS; MHT follows standard rules and PMOS is not a contraindication; no extra cancer screening or DXA program
What are we watching for, and how often?
T2D several-fold at any weight; CVD OR ~1.7; endometrial cancer 2–3× from unopposed estrogen; pregnancy complications; depression, anxiety, disordered eating; OSA and MASLD
OGTT q1–3 yr; annual lipids/BP/mood; PHQ-9/GAD-7 every visit
Is a life circumstance turning a correct plan into a failed one?
Missed refills, weight regain, worse OGTT, declined CHC, cancelled visits each get a probe before the plan changes; contextualized plans improved outcomes (NNT ~6 per red flag)
